why: The standalone please. Carried on its own rather than as a suffix, because it does not mark the speaker's gender and so it is the one politeness word usable without a choice.
caution: Weaker than ครับ/ค่ะ and it can sound flat to a stranger. Use it when you cannot or do not want to pick a gender form.

why: Works for thanks, for apology, for 'excuse me' in a doorway, and for 'goodbye' to a shopkeeper. Getting this one right buys you goodwill everywhere.
caution: Do not translate คุณ as the English 'you' when counting things -- here it is just part of the word. ขอบคุณมาก ('thank you very much') exists too but is not needed at Tier 0; plain ขอบคุณ with a smile already reads as sincere.

why: One word doing two jobs -- getting someone's attention ('excuse me') and apologising ('I am sorry'). A traveller needs both constantly, so both glosses live here.
caution: It is close to neutral in tone, not apologetic. Do not use it as a deep apology for a real mistake; Thais apologise more with พิษมา (pis-ma) plus a wai, not with ขอโทษ alone.

text_native: คุณชื่ออะไร
why: How you ask someone's name. คุณ is the safe polite address word for a stranger of any gender, which is why this question needs no pronoun.
caution: Expect a first name only, and expect to be addressed by nickname afterwards. Surnames are rarely used to address people in Thailand. Answering with ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก (entry 17) is the natural reply.

why: The reassuring answer to a shopkeeper or a host, and the neutral way to decline something gently.
caution: None, which is rare and worth recording.

why: The all-purpose agreement. Also the word used to close a price negotiation, which is why it matters more in transactions than it looks.
caution: Overused it becomes a way to end a conversation you did not mean to end.

text_native: พูดช้าๆ หน่อย
why: The second thing to try after ไม่เข้าใจ. Tone is genuinely polite here -- ช้าๆ means 'a little slow', not 'slow'. In Thai a bare command to slow down would sound rude.
caution: The หน่อย softens the whole sentence. Without it, พูดช้าๆ to an older person is borderline; with it, it is a normal request.

text_native: พูดภาษาอังกฤษได้ไหม
why: The question that changes the whole trip. In a city it gets you English; in a village it gets you a smile and a shrug instead.
caution: The trailing ไหม marks it as a question and wants a rising tone on ไห. Put it at the end. คุณ at the front is optional politeness.

text_native: พูดภาษาไทยไม่ได้
why: Saying this buys enormous goodwill. Thais routinely speak a little English to foreigners and expect nothing back; naming the gap yourself removes the awkwardness.
caution: Note there is no 'I' in this phrase. Thai drops the first-person pronoun when the context makes it obvious, which is also how you avoid having to choose between the male ผม and the female ดิฉัน.

why: The single most useful phrase when nothing else works. Replaces the dropped 'try again', which asked for effort rather than asking for the thing actually needed.
caution: Saying it louder does not work. Thai does not raise volume for emphasis the way English does; the request has to be repeated as words.

text_native: ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก
text_romanized: yin di thi dai ru jak
why: The stock phrase after names are exchanged, and one of the first full Thai sentences a visitor tends to recognise when it is aimed at them.
caution: It is polite but not stiff, so it will never offend. Expect to hear it back at you if you answer คุณชื่ออะไร with your own name.

why: The standard explicit goodbye, 'I take my leave'. Works in every register and needs no pronoun.
caution: Do not pair it with ครับ or ค่ะ unless one matches your own gender. When in doubt just say สวัสดี again as your goodbye -- Thais often treat สวัสดี as both hello and bye.

why: The reply to สบายดีหรือ and also the reply to 'Are you all right?' in an emergency. One word carries both.
caution: Same word, same spelling as the middle of entry 5. Tone changes the meaning: this ดี is high tone. RTGS cannot show that, so listen to a native rather than reading the romanisation for tone.

text_native: สบายดีหรือ
why: Literally 'are you well or not'. It is the standard opener after สวัสดี and needs no reply beyond one word.
caution: Read as a flat statement, not with English rising question intonation -- Wikivoyage warns that foreigners should not inflect questions upward. Tone matters here: ดี here must be mid tone. Say 'di' flat and it is right; say it with a sharp falling tone and it does not scan.

why: The word you will need most and can use with anyone, any age, any status. It covers hello, hi, good morning, good afternoon and good evening all at once, so one item does the work of five.
caution: Not gender-marked on its own, which is why it is the safest opener. Add ครับ or ค่ะ (entries 3 and 4) if you want to sound polite to a stranger.

text_native: สวัสดีครับ
why: The polite form of hello for a male speaker. ครับ marks the speaker's gender, so this is only correct if you are a man.
caution: Saying ครับ as a woman, or ค่ะ as a man, is the single most obvious mistake a foreigner makes in Thai. If you are unsure of your own Thai gender register, use bare สวัสดี (entry 1) -- it is never wrong.

why: The polite form of hello for a female speaker. ค่ะ marks the speaker's gender, so this is only correct if you are a woman.
caution: Do not use ค่ะ as a male speaker. Note RTGS drops the tone, so ค่ะ is romanised 'kha' and not 'khaa' or 'khá' -- the rising tone on ค่ is what distinguishes it.

why: The positive of ไม่เข้าใจ, and the honest way to end a sequence of misunderstandings.
caution: Claiming it when you do not is the single most expensive thing a learner can do in this language, because the conversation then continues in Thai and stops being survivable.

why: Almost never the answer you want. Thai marks negation on the verb, so 'yes' is usually the verb repeated rather than this word.
caution: Answering a yes/no question with ใช่ to a Thai is odd, not wrong, but it reads as a foreigner who has memorised a list. Wikivoyage says outright that foreigners are taught this and it is more complicated.

why: Saying this plainly is much better than improvising. Included as the honest fallback when a phrase is missing.
caution: Wikivoyage pairs it with the formal ไม่ทราบ. The plain form is the right one for a learner; the formal one is not wrong, just stiff.

why: The most useful four syllables in the language. Say it and a Thai speaker will normally switch to English, gesture, or slow down.
caution: Its opposite, เข้าใจ (khao chai), is what you will hear when they have understood -- worth recognising so you know to stop speaking.

text_english: You are welcome / It is all right
why: The all-purpose answer: 'no problem', 'it is all right', 'you are welcome', 'never mind'. Wikivoyage calls it the national motto of Thailand.
caution: The real trap: in reply to a complaint it can mean 'it's not my problem' or 'it shouldn't worry you'. If you say it after being overcharged, the listener may hear you as shrugging. The phrasebook flags exactly this.

why: The negative of ใช่, with the same caveat: it means 'not right' or 'is not', not a general 'no'.
caution: Same trap as ใช่. To refuse something, Thai negates the verb — ไม่เอา, ไม่ซื้อ — and this word is not the general word for refusing.

why: The only time word the surviving content had. It also opens a request: ตอนนี้ plus a verb is a perfectly good way to ask for something immediately.
One word that unlocks the two questions a traveller asks most in Thailand: is the night market on today, and is the temple open today.
caution: It is a time word, not a courtesy word, so it needs a verb around it -- 'วันนี้ไปตลาดไหม' (go to the market today?). As a bare word with a flat tone it can also be read as an emphatic 'today!'

text_native: นี่เท่าไหร่
why: Point at the thing and say this. The phrasebook's version, with นี่ meaning 'this (here)', is the general form -- unlike the longer bitext sentences about specific goods.
caution: Point to the item as you say it; นี่ on its own will not identify anything. Thai has no question inflection, so say it flat.

why: The bare price question, unattached to any noun. Replaces the dropped per-kilo form, which was a specific counter phrase rather than the word a traveller reaches for.
caution: Thai needs a classifier between the noun and the price in formal speech; bare เท่าไหร่ is understood everywhere and is the safe form for a learner.

why: What you will hear when a price is too high. Knowing the single word tells you whether to negotiate, and the phrasebook's fuller แพงไป ('too expensive') carries the same message with more edge.
caution: A tone-flat แพง is a statement of fact. To make it a complaint rather than an observation, the pitch has to do the work that intonation does in English -- so do not expect the romanisation to help you here.

why: In Thailand 'water' means room-temperature still water, not ice water. น้ำเปล่า is what you will be handed, and it is the phrase on the menu for plain water.
caution: If you want ice, ask for น้ำเย็น (nam yen, cold water) or น้ำแข็ง (nam khaeng, ice water); neither is in this Tier 0 set because neither is attested in the two sources used. Saying น้ำเปล่า when you actually want ice is the usual beginner error.

why: One syllable that gets you fed. Far more economical than a sentence, and Thais respond to it immediately.
caution: Same word as หิวน้ำ ('thirsty') plus น้ำ, so a mispronunciation of the second syllable will turn your hunger into thirst.

why: The pairing that gets a drink ordered. หิว alone is only hunger; the water word is what turns it into a request.
The word a Thai expects to hear after eating, and saying it is worth more to the person cooking than the meal is.
A feeling word a traveller needs to hear more often than to say, and one that shortens an interaction politely.
The noun, standing in for the dropped 'take the bus' verb phrase. Nouns are the safer half of a transport phrase for a learner to recognise.
caution: Saying the noun on its own does not order a bus; it identifies one.

text_native: จะไป _____ อย่างไร
why: The general 'how do I get to X' frame. จะไป means 'will go' and อย่างไร means 'in what manner' -- future-tense 'will' plus 'how', not 'go how'.
caution: There is no word for 'please' in the frame; politeness in this request is the flat tone, not a particle, so adding ครับ or ค่ะ here is optional rather than required. The attested bitext sentence for the same idea is far longer and much harder to say.

why: Completes the minimum directional set: left, right, straight on. Note there is no 'ahead' word -- ไป alone carries 'go'.
caution: Literally 'straight go'. It is only correct when the road genuinely continues straight; for 'keep going until the junction' you need ตรงไป until a ก่อนถึง (before reaching) phrase, which is outside Tier 0.

why: The word that matters most in an unfamiliar building, and the one a learner most needs to be able to read rather than say.
Sign vocabulary. Included because a traveller reads signs long before they can read anything else.
The bare 'where', and the single most reusable question in the language.
caution: Needs a tone mark a learner cannot hear themselves produce; the mark on ไหน is what separates this from several other common words.

why: The noun you drop into entry 29's frame: 'จะไปสถานีรถไฟอย่างไร'. Also the word on every sign and timetable you need.
caution: สถานี means station in general, so a bus station is สถานีรถโดยสาร and an airport is สนามบิน; saying only สถานี will be understood but will not tell the driver which one you mean.

why: The word on the sign, the word in the entry 28 question, and the word you need to read rather than say.
caution: Read as ห้องน้ำ you will find it on its own or as ห้องสุขา (hong sukha), which is the older, more formal version used on government buildings.

text_native: ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหน
why: The single most useful question in Thailand for a traveller. Word order is subject-verb-place, so the sentence is 'toilet is at where' -- no 'is' and no inversion.
caution: Say it flat, not rising. 'ห้องน้ำอยู่' means 'the toilet is at / is located'; เป็น would be for a thing that is rather than sits somewhere, and getting that wrong is a common beginner tell. Wikivoyage writes it with spaces (ห้องน้ำ อยู่ ที่ ไหน); Thai does not use word spaces, so it is written solid here.

why: The bare 'what'. Included because a learner who knows one word can use it to make any question, which is worth more at Tier 0 than a long phrase they will not remember.
caution: Attaching it to a noun changes the meaning unpredictably. Kept standalone for that reason.

why: The bare 'when', for opening and bus times.
caution: Time in Thailand runs on a 24-hour official clock in transport, so a bare 'when' often needs a number attached.

why: The mirror of entry 31 and the other half of the common เลี้ยวซ้ายเลี้ยวขวา ('left right'), which you can say while you are still deciding.
caution: ขวา is a short syllable; miss the consonant and it becomes ขวา as in 'narrow'. Pair it with a hand gesture at first -- pointing the right way is understood even when the word is not.

text_native: เลี้ยวซ้าย
why: The first direction command most travellers need. It is also one half of the very useful เลี้ยวซ้ายเลี้ยวขวา, which some use purely to signal indecision at a junction.
caution: Left and right are from the speaker's point of view, not the driver's, and Thailand drives on the left, so a taxi driver's 'left' can feel like your right. This is the standard way-round moment for visitors.

text_native: ซื้อไม่ไหว
why: A real way to decline a price that keeps the interaction polite. Replaces the dropped 'I have no money', which is both ruder and less useful.
caution: Wikivoyage's version carries a gendered pronoun; only the verb phrase is kept here.

why: The word a learner needs in order to recognise a bargain when one is offered.
caution: Learners overuse it as a bargaining opener, which is read as a comment on the shop rather than an offer.

why: The complete phrase, where แพง on its own is just the adjective 'expensive'. Shows how a particle changes a label into a complaint.
caution: Said flatly it can end the negotiation. It is a statement, not an opening bid.

text_native: กระเป๋าสตางค์
why: The noun you name in a lost-property report. You will also hear it back from police and transport staff when they ask what you lost.
caution: Colloquially people just say กระเป๋าเงิน ('money bag') for a purse. That variant is not in this Tier 0 set because it is not attested in either of the two sources used.

why: The verb phrase from Wikivoyage's 'I need a doctor', with the gendered pronoun stripped so it is usable by anyone. ขอ ('request') is itself a softener. SOURCED honestly: Wikivoyage writes this as ผม/ดิฉัน ต้องการหมอ, which hardcodes a gendered pronoun. Stripping the pronoun and keeping ต้องการหมอ would have been the lift; this uses ขอ ('request') instead, which is a composition rather than a quotation, so it is recorded as `authored` and not as `curated`. Both ขอ and หมอ are on the Wikivoyage page; the pairing is LangKraft's.
caution: ขอ is a request, not a demand, and works with a doctor as well as with a waiter.

why: The distress call. Loud, unmistakable, and the phrase that makes bystanders act.
caution: It is a shout, not a sentence. There is no pronoun and no politeness marker in it, which is correct for an emergency -- but do not use it for small problems or you will get exactly the response you asked for.

why: The bare noun, shouted on its own and the word on police stations, police boxes and uniforms. Useful both to recognise and to use as a shout.
caution: Do not shout ตำรวจ at a waiter to get attention -- it means 'police' with no softening particle, so it gets a reaction rather than a meal.

text_native: ต้องการหมอ
why: The phrase that gets you to a clinic, a hospital desk, or a hotel receptionist who can ring one. Short enough to say badly.
caution: ต้อง means 'must' and is not optional in this sentence. The attested source sentence supplies a first-person pronoun (ผม or ดิฉัน); it has been dropped here so the phrase works for any speaker.

why: What someone shouts at you from a motorbike seconds before it clips you. Hearing it and stepping aside is the whole point of knowing it.
caution: It is a bare warning with no particle, which is why it can be shouted by a stranger and why it works. A listener who knows this word is noticeably safer in Bangkok than one who does not.

why: One syllable carries the entire report: 'กระเป๋าสตางค์ของผมหาย' is 'my wallet is gone'. Short enough to say while panicking.
caution: Attaching หาย to the thing is what makes it a loss report; on its own, to a person, it just means 'they are gone'. The attested bitext sentence for losing a wallet also carries a stray ทำ (the verb 'to do'), so that full sentence was left out as it would have shipped a typo.

text_native: เรื่องฉุกเฉิน
why: The phrase that changes how fast people move. Replaces the dropped 'call the police', which named a specific institution rather than the situation.
caution: It does not replace actually phoning anyone. It is for the room you are standing in.

why: The one word that describes an emergency instead of requesting help. Combine it with ช่วยด้วย when you are the one in trouble.
caution: It also means the physical fire or a lighter, so it appears in unexpected places; context tells you which. Do not use it for a small flame such as a candle or a cigarette -- a shout of ไฟไหม้ in a restaurant causes a real evacuation.

why: The single most important social sound in the language for a man. It marks you as polite, and it is what makes people wait until you have finished instead of walking past.
caution: It marks the SPEAKER's gender, not the listener's. Using ครับ as a woman is a clear error. RTGS writes it 'khrap' with no tone mark -- the written ครับ carries a low tone that a learner must hear rather than read.

why: The all-purpose polite address word for a stranger of any gender, and the word that opens คุณชื่ออะไร. You will hear it many times a day; using it means you never have to guess Mr or Mrs.
caution: Do not use it for close friends or for anyone much younger than you in an informal setting -- it reads as cold. Do not translate it as the English 'you' when it is part of a compound such as ขอบคุณ, where it is not a separate word.

why: The female-speaker equivalent of ครับ, and the ending that turns a bare request into a polite one.
caution: It marks the SPEAKER's gender, not the listener's, and it is not interchangeable with ครับ. In questions a shorter variant คะ is used instead -- neither ค่ะ nor ครับ is required in a question.

why: The counterpart to พี่, and the correct way to attract a waiter who looks younger than you, where English 'excuse me' would sound odd.
caution: Like พี่ it is always used with a first name and it is more than 'young' -- it carries seniority, so a 30-year-old may call a 25-year-old น้อง.

why: How you address someone older than you who you know informally, and how you attract a waiter who looks older than you. Thais use it for much older people than English 'older' suggests.
caution: Always used with a first name -- พี่สมชาย, never a surname. Calling a stranger พี่ without a name sounds incomplete, and using it towards someone who resents the age gap is not harmless.
